response.reasoning: Ninety-three units over 12,311 words covers the argument, all fifteen definitions, the mechanism, the secondary fields, the evaluation protocol and the evidence register. Walking the document again against them, the gaps are concentrated in three places: the exemplars attached to each definition, the parts of the pairwise table I grouped rather than split, and the worked example sentences the codebook uses to fix a boundary. Those examples are load-bearing in a codebook -- a rater applies the exemplar, not the abstract cue -- so their absence is a real loss rather than a cosmetic one.

findings.description: Every one of the fifteen definitions carries two exemplars -- one document-style, one conversational -- and none of them is extracted. The specification states that exemplars are part of the required shape of a definition, and codebook evidence in the same document says concretely-described features outperform interpretive ones. A consumer retrieving a definition without its exemplars gets the half that measured worse.

Several pairwise separations are grouped into a single unit covering six boundaries at once. Each is independently applicable and independently citable -- a rater resolving observation versus event does not want the formula/definition rule in the same record. The grouping trades retrievability for compactness in the one section the document says is the bulk of a working codebook.

candidates.title: Statement classifier codebook: the fifteen label definitions
candidates.summary: The fifteen fine labels, each carried with the surface cue that fires it and the exclusions that stop it. These are the operative content of the codebook: the specification's own evidence is that definitions, not label count, determine whether the classifier works, so each is stated here in full rather than described.

assertions.text: `observation` (coarse `case`, anchor κ 0.79) fires on an insight extrapolated from multiple events -- a pattern or reading drawn across more than one occasion, anecdotal by nature in that it holds so far on what has been seen, and not definitive enough to be a rule or a recommendation. A single occurrence reported as fact is an `event`; it becomes an `observation` when the sentence reads across occasions through a rate, a repetition, a sample, a trend or a mean.

`event` (coarse `case`) fires on a single thing that happened, reported as fact: singular and factual. Quantity does not disqualify it -- an incident report full of counts and losses is still one occurrence. It excludes a reading drawn from what happened, which is an `observation`.

`obligation` (coarse `method`) fires on what is owed to a third party: a requirement is an `obligation` only when there is someone outside the doing party to whom it is owed -- a regulator, an exchange, a counterparty, a client, a contract. It is the positive counterpart of `prohibition`, and excludes what must not be done and internal requirements.

`prohibition` (coarse `method`) is the negative case of `procedure`: where a `procedure` says what to do, a `prohibition` says what must not be done. It is a hard rule, manual-grade -- it would be printed as an absolute and it can be violated. The test is whether someone could be in breach of it.

`decision` (coarse `method`) fires on a choice reported as settled which governs what happens after it -- typically past-tense and agentive: adopted, chose, approved, standardised on, agreed to. It is the one `rule` label with no deontic modal to key on, which is why it needs its own surface cues.

`procedure` (coarse `method`, anchor κ 0.74) fires on an established operational instruction -- how the system is used. The test is whether it could be pasted into a user manual unchanged and read as something to be followed every time. The discriminating question is whether the sentence reports practice or puts something forward; anything put forward is excluded.

`recommendation` (coarse `method`) prescribes a course of action -- advice on what ought to be done, with no requirement force and nothing settled. It is practical and experiential, bearing on a choice where more than one valid option exists, and usually conversational in register. It excludes a requirement someone is accountable to.

`definition` (coarse `concept`, anchor κ 0.81) fixes a key topic: it states what a term means and the term is load-bearing -- remove the definition and the reader cannot follow what follows. The grammatical centre is 'X is / means / refers to / is defined as Y'. It excludes a contingent statement that could turn out false.

`distinction` (coarse `concept`) fires on a qualifier between multiple methods or options, resting on established differences rather than on one occasion's measurement. The contrast is the payload: two things are named and what separates them is the point. It excludes a single term being defined.

`background` (coarse `concept`, anchor κ 0.87) fires on additional colour or history: it enriches understanding of the surround but does not define the topic itself. Strip it out and the topic is still defined; you have only lost context. Its excludes list is simply 'everything else', which is the point -- it is defined as the residual of the `concept` family.

`principle` (coarse `model`) fires on the theory or rule behind something -- reasoning from fundamentals about why it holds or why it is built that way. First principles, not comparison, not measurement, and not implementation. The test is whether it would survive without the specific case in front of you.

`architecture` (coarse `system`) fires on implementational design -- the construction of a physical or software system: what it is built out of, what components it has, what they are. It is not a logical scheme and not a configuration, and it excludes how the system is used.

`assumption` (coarse `model`) fires on a leap of faith -- something taken on trust for the rest to hold, asserted without evidence and without proof, where the sentence knows it. Marker words are assumes, presupposes, conditional on, holds only if, provided that, on the standing assumption that. It excludes something needed to run rather than to be true.

`dependency` (coarse `system`) fires on an established requirement -- a hard fact that the thing cannot run without. Marker words are requires, depends on, needs, is a prerequisite for, and 'without X you cannot'. It excludes something taken for granted for a claim to hold, which is an `assumption`.

[VERIFIED] Within a single annotation scheme, per-category reliability varies by a factor of two, and the abstract categories are systematically worst: CoreSC measured Conclusion 0.89, Background 0.87, Object 0.81, Observation 0.79, Result 0.78 and Method 0.74, against Hypothesis 0.46, Motivation 0.46 and Model 0.43.

[DESIGN] Merging `conclusion` into `finding` cuts against the other change in the same revision: `finding` already took 24% of all assignments and was behaving as a de-facto residual, so widening it increases that risk. The merged definition therefore tightens its exclusions against `fact` and `observation` rather than loosening them, and whether that holds is a re-test rather than a claim.

The status ladder has four rungs, each adding a different thing: `floated` puts a point on the table, `proposed` adds specification, `evidenced` adds evidence, and `settled` adds certainty. The test separating the first two is whether you could act on the sentence as written or would first have to invent the parameters.

[DESIGN] Provenance is a separate field and is not classified, because where a record came from is known at ingestion and costs no agreement -- it cannot be got wrong by a model that never infers it. It is distinct from status: status says how firmly a statement is held now, provenance says where it was born. Both are worth having; only one of them can be got wrong.

[DESIGN] The reassurance marker routes to `recommendation` on the reasoning that procedures and principles do not have feelings: language that soothes, warns off or manages the reader's reaction -- don't panic, no need to worry, don't stress, ignore me -- marks the sentence as advice from a person rather than an operational instruction or a standing relation.

Several separations are single discriminating questions: `observation`/`event` asks whether anything was measured; `event`/`decision` whether a choice was made; `principle`/`architecture` asks WHY it works versus HOW it is built, resolved by whether deleting the sentence would leave you unable to explain the idea or unable to rebuild the thing; `assumption`/`dependency` asks must-be-TRUE versus must-be-PRESENT; `formula`/`definition` asks whether it computes; and `definition`/`distinction` asks whether one term or two.

The model answers one independent yes/no question per fine label in a single call and is never asked to pick one of fifteen. `form` takes statement, question or answer, is orthogonal to type and available under every coarse category -- a question about a procedure is type procedure, form question. candidates.title: Statement classifier: contract, scope and evidence conventions
candidates.summary: What the classifier promises, what it refuses to do, and how every claim in its specification is evidenced.

assertions.text: The classifier's contract is one statement in, one classification record out, with an optional context argument. The context is used to classify that statement -- a line is often only readable against what came before -- but never to reclassify the neighbours themselves. [DESIGN] This reverses an earlier restriction that limited context to pronoun and ellipsis resolution, because several statements measured as unclassifiable in isolation are unambiguous in place.

[MEASURED] Three separate in-house results form one pattern: confidence-based abstention lost, booleans plus priority resolution lost 0.092, and interior tiers lost 0.11. Anything that turns one classification decision into two costs more in the second step than it gains in the first.

[MEASURED] Status is dependent on type but does not collapse into it: Cramér's V = 0.595 with mutual information 0.845 of 1.721 bits, so 49% of status is predictable from type and 51% is not. This test was run because the published two-axis design the spec cites failed when its axes turned out statistically dependent and collapsed into a few cells.

[VERIFIED] Definitions must be written as surface tests rather than judgment calls: concretely-described features reached F1 above 0.60 while features requiring interpretive inference fell below 0.30, and model difficulty tracked human inter-coder difficulty at r = 0.61 -- so human disagreement is the practical ceiling. Measured over 7 models, 121 features and 567 excerpts.

Every one of the fifteen definitions carries the same three-part shape: a **Cue** stating the surface pattern so a reader can check it without inferring intent, an **Excludes** list with at least two explicit non-firing conditions, and **Exemplars** giving one document-style statement and one conversational. Pairwise separations live in a single section rather than inside each definition, so a boundary is stated once and cannot drift between two entries.

`formula` (coarse `model`) fires on something mathematical or scientific in nature -- an equation, an arithmetic definition in prose, or a statement defining something in mathematical or scientific terms. A `formula` says what a quantity equals and instructs nobody. The test is whether the arithmetic is the payload or machinery inside a policy.

[VERIFIED] Presenting options as A/B/C/D inherits selection bias, and most of the effect comes from the option-ID tokens rather than position: removing the IDs cut recall standard deviation from 5.5 to 1.0 on MMLU, shuffling does not fix it, and a debiasing instruction barely helps (Zheng et al., 20 models). Tests are therefore emitted as named boolean fields -- no lettered options and no ordered menu.

`modality` takes required, permitted or prohibited and is populated whenever a deontic modal is present, independent of which type test fired. It is validated only on statements that resolved to `rule` and otherwise retained but not enforced. [DESIGN] There is no measured evidence for it: deontic modals are surface cues, which is the property associated with reliable categories, but this specific field has not been evaluated.

[DESIGN] Two flags are carried: `negative_result` for a statement reporting an absence, null or no-effect finding, and `caveat` for one that limits, scopes or excepts something else. Neither has measured evidence. `negative_result` exists because a null finding is not distinguishable from a positive one by embedding similarity -- 'X does not work' and 'X works' are near neighbours -- so without an explicit marker it is unrecoverable downstream. That is a mechanism argument, not a measurement.

[VERIFIED] The strongest direct evidence about typed information is negative and human: two controlled experiments on a shipped information-typing scheme found no effect on task performance -- n=65 process operators, effectiveness F(2,62)=1.16 p=.32, efficiency F(2,62)=2.02 p=.14; and n=76 with no significant effects on accuracy, speed or evaluation scores at all. The only significant effect was subjective preference, and even that did not beat the incumbent text.

The scope limit on the null result, raised by all three verifiers, is that those studies were powered for large effects only and typing was bundled with six other principles -- so this is absence of a large effect, not proof that typing is inert. [VERIFIED] Separately, no source in the reviewed evidence isolates type labels from anything else: every system claiming a typing benefit bundles it with linking, extraction, reranking or temporal invalidation, and the counterfactual -- same corpus, same retriever, labels stripped -- has never been run. The one payoff replicating across three independent agent-memory systems is temporal validity, not typing.

A kill criterion is pre-registered before the classifier may be treated as load-bearing: run the ablation on the same corpus, same retriever and same ranking with type labels present versus stripped, pre-registering the query classes and minimum effect size; user preference does not count as a gain, written down before results exist because the one scheme that shipped on preference failed on task; and if no query class improves, the classifier is decoration -- keep temporal validity and drop the rest.

The specification labels every claim by what backs it: [VERIFIED] survived three-vote adversarial verification against a named primary source with the study, number and sample given inline; [MEASURED] comes from in-house runs that measured this codebook rather than a published one; and [DESIGN] marks an engineering decision with no supporting measurement at all. Nothing is presented as evidence-backed unless a number is attached.

candidates.title: Statement classifier: the gaps its designers left open
candidates.summary: Named, unclosed gaps: content with no home in the taxonomy, work deliberately out of scope for v1, and questions where the search for evidence returned nothing that survived verification.

assertions.text: The classifier answers 'what kind of statement is this' and never 'is this correct'. Truth judgment is explicitly out of scope, and epistemic status lives in a separate field rather than in the type.

Permission-shaped statements have no home in the taxonomy. A sentence such as 'Analysts may exceed the intraday limit provided the book is flat at close' carries a deontic modal but is neither required nor prohibited, so it will land in `general` or be pulled into `obligation` by the modal. The specification directs watching `general`'s share on permission-heavy corpora such as policy documents.

No evidence was found on three questions the design needs answered: resolving pronouns and ellipsis before classification, splitting one message into several statements, and how much surrounding context a conversational statement needs. Three separate research angles returned nothing that survived verification, and the only context datapoint anywhere in the evidence base is a 20–30 line window used as an unablated design choice.

[DESIGN] The consequences for conversational input are that it may carry an optional context window used only for reference resolution, a statement whose references cannot be resolved is classified `general` rather than guessed, splitting a multi-statement message is out of scope for v1 with the caller supplying one statement, and conversational accuracy is expected materially below document accuracy and must be measured separately.

The classifier produces no truth judgment and no relationships between statements. Epistemic maturity is produced -- that is `status` -- but whether a statement is correct is not, and neither are edges between statements. Relations such as resolved_by and opposes are named as the natural next layer and are deliberately out of scope for v1.
